findings.summary: A stray one-word line "Spaces" sits before the actual bullet and reads as a dangling heading.
findings.evidence: "Spaces" followed by "Spaces need quotes or a backslash: cd \"My Docs\" or cd My\ Docs"
findings.fix: Remove the standalone "Spaces" line, or make it a proper labelled subheading, and keep the single bullet.

findings.summary: The ls-before-rm safety check is split into disconnected fragments instead of a clear ordered flow.
findings.evidence: "ls /path/ check the target rm -r /path/ no undo Danger line rm -rf /path/ is the one to fear."
findings.fix: Show it as a two-step flow (ls /path/ -> check -> rm -r /path/) with the warning as one separate bullet.

findings.summary: The usermod command appears before the idea it illustrates, and its explanation is a fragment after the code.
findings.evidence: "bash sudo usermod -aG docker alice" followed by "without -a, other groups are dropped; log in again"
findings.fix: State the idea first ("-aG appends a group to a user"), then show the code. Put the -a warning and the re-login note in separate bullets.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "directory", "argument").
findings.evidence: Mistake: ln -s argument order is target first, then link name; a relative symlink target is resolved from the link's folder, not your current directory
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The 'Cross fs / dirs' row says hard links cannot cross directories, but hard links can sit in different directories. The real restriction is that they cannot point at directories.
findings.evidence: Cross fs / dirs | no | yes
findings.fix: Split the row in two: 'Across filesystems: no | yes' and 'Can target a directory: no | yes'. Hard links may live in any directory of the same filesystem.

findings.summary: Cheat-sheet bullets pack several unrelated commands or ideas into one line, which hurts skimming.
findings.evidence: "chmod u+x f; chown user:group f (new owner needs root)" and "Hard link: second name, same inode. Symlink: a path pointer"
findings.fix: Split each into one bullet per idea, or move the hard link vs symlink contrast into a two-row table.

findings.summary: The Mistakes section is a prose sentence holding two separate mistakes.
findings.evidence: "chmod -R 755 makes plain files executable: use X. usermod without -a drops other groups."
findings.fix: Write two one-line bullets, one per mistake, each with its fix.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "standard", "workflow").
findings.evidence: Standard workflow: run a long command, press Ctrl+Z, run bg to keep it running, then run fg to return to it
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The jobs bullet shows '[1]+' without saying what it marks, so a skimmer could misread it as the job number.
findings.evidence: jobs lists this shell's jobs as [1]+
findings.fix: State that [1] is the job number and + marks the current job, or show a sample jobs output line.

findings.summary: The exit-code table ends with a row that is not an exit code, so the table mixes two kinds of content.
findings.evidence: echo $? | last command's code
findings.fix: Move 'echo $? prints the last command's code' out of the table into a one-line bullet under it.

findings.summary: Several cheat-sheet bullets pack multiple ideas into one line, which is hard to skim.
findings.evidence: ps aux / ps -ef: snapshot; pgrep -a name: find PIDs
findings.fix: Split into one bullet per command, or use a Command | Use table.

findings.summary: The jobs line in the code block holds three separate actions in a comment, and the exit-code table drops the 128+N rule that page 4 states.
findings.evidence: jobs                  # Ctrl+Z, bg %n, fg %n
findings.fix: Put the job-control keys in their own table or bullets, and add a 128+N row to the exit-code table.

findings.summary: One bullet packs three separate flags (-F, -w, -o) into a single line.
findings.evidence: -F literal text, -w whole words, -o only the match
findings.fix: Split into three one-line bullets, or add -F, -w and -o to the flag table, with each code example next to its flag.

findings.summary: Bullets combine unrelated ideas, so a skimmer must parse two facts per line.
findings.evidence: uniq -c counts; uniq -d shows only duplicates
findings.fix: Move uniq -c and uniq -d into a small flag table or split them into separate bullets.

findings.summary: The common mistakes are a bare list of fragments with no reason or fix next to each.
findings.evidence:
Useless cat file | grep x: use grep x file
uniq without sort
Unquoted patterns
xargs rm without previewing
findings.fix: Turn it into a two-column table (Mistake | Fix or why), e.g. 'uniq without sort | only adjacent duplicates collapse'.

findings.summary: The flag table puts an example command inside the Effect column, which mixes explanation with code.
findings.evidence: -I{} | places the argument anywhere: xargs -I{} cp {} /backup
findings.fix: Keep the Effect cell to the one-line idea and put the cp example in the bash block.

findings.summary: Table rows contain a literal pipe character, which makes the columns ambiguous when skimming.
findings.evidence:
cmd | tee f | write file, pass on
Count | sort | uniq -c
findings.fix: Put the tee row in its own code line or note, and use a different layout (e.g. code-formatted cells) for rows whose commands contain pipes.

findings.summary: The recipes line is a prose list that names the recipes before the code, and the code block does not match it one-to-one.
findings.evidence: Top-N, safe delete (preview with echo), count matches
findings.fix: Replace the line with a comment above each command in the bash block, e.g. '# Top-N', '# preview delete', '# count matches'.

findings.summary: The variables code block comes before the idea behind it, and one bullet holds two ideas.
findings.evidence: Untyped strings; global unless local in a function
findings.fix: State the one-line idea first (variables are untyped strings). Put scope in its own bullet: 'global by default; local limits it to a function'.

findings.summary: Test syntax is covered on page 2, before conditionals are introduced on page 3. It also packs two ideas into one bullet.
findings.evidence: [[ ]]: left side needs no quotes; == is pattern match
findings.fix: Move the [ ] vs [[ ]] quoting notes to page 3's comparison table. Give pattern match its own bullet.

findings.summary: The chapter says `[[ ]]` is a command returning a status, but `[[` is a shell keyword, and the same page's interview answer calls it a keyword.
findings.evidence: "[ ] and [[ ]] are just commands returning a status" vs. "POSIX command vs bash keyword: no splitting, &&, =~"
findings.fix: Write: "`[` is a command (a builtin, also found as /usr/bin/[) and `[[ ]]` is a bash keyword; both give an exit status that `if` tests."

findings.summary: One bullet holds two ideas and reads cryptically.
findings.evidence: Why while read -r? for over $(cat f) splits on spaces; -r keeps backslashes
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: 'for over $(cat f) splits on spaces; use while read' and '-r keeps backslashes literal'.

findings.summary: The cron troubleshooting is a run-on prose paragraph with several separate fixes, where one-line bullets would do.
findings.evidence: Cron has a minimal PATH and no login environment. Use absolute paths, set PATH= at the top, and add >> /var/log/job.log 2>&1 or output mail is lost.
findings.fix: Split into bullets: cause (minimal PATH, no login env); fix 1 absolute paths; fix 2 set PATH= at the top; fix 3 redirect output with >> /var/log/job.log 2>&1 so it isn't mailed away.

findings.summary: One bullet holds two separate set -e exceptions, with the example crammed in.
findings.evidence: Also skips any &&/|| command except the last: false && x lives, true && false exits
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: 'set -e ignores a failing non-last command in an &&/|| list' (example: false && x lives) and 'a failing last command still exits' (example: true && false exits).

findings.summary: The cron field names dom, mon and dow are used on page 5 without being defined. The page 6 cron section is also a broken list instead of a table.
findings.evidence: Page 5: 'Fields: min hour dom mon dow command'. Page 6: 'm / min / h / hour / dom / day / mon / month / dow / weekday / cmd / command' as alternating one-line entries
findings.fix: Render the cron fields as a table (Field | Meaning | Range) or a single annotated line, and define dom/dow where first introduced. Put the schedule examples in a Schedule | Runs table, as on page 5.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "interview", "skeleton").
findings.evidence: Interview Point: Write a safe script skeleton from memory. What breaks if you omit quotes? How would you debug a failing cron job?
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The layer stack is a run of one-word lines, so the order and the pairing of layer to tool are unclear.
findings.evidence:
IP on interface
ip
Route
gateway
DNS
dig
Port
ss, curl
Firewall
allows it
findings.fix: Replace the lines with a table (Layer | Check | Tool) or a top-to-bottom diagram, and show the bottom-up debug order as numbered steps.

findings.summary: The debug order in section 3 leaves out the firewall layer, which section 1 lists as the last layer to check.
findings.evidence: Section 1 ends with "Firewall allows it" and "Debug bottom-up in that order". Section 3 ends at "curl -v service answers?" and has no firewall step.
findings.fix: Add a final firewall step to the ordered checklist, for example "ufw status / security group: is the port allowed?".

findings.summary: One table row packs three unrelated flags and three ideas into a single bullet.
findings.evidence: -X -H -d | method, header, JSON body
findings.fix: Split it into three rows: -X sets the method, -H adds a header, -d sends the body.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "production", "running").
findings.evidence: scp -p vs -P, running ss without sudo (no process names shown), and using curl -k in production. Use nc -zv host port to test whether a TCP port is open.
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The term 'security group' is used as a firewall layer, but no page ever defines it.
findings.evidence: Timeout | Firewall or security group drops packets, or bad route; ufw allow 8080 alone: cloud security group or router still blocks
findings.fix: Add one line on page 5: a security group is the cloud provider's firewall in front of the instance, managed outside the host, so it must also allow the port.

findings.summary: The wording is ambiguous: "unreachable either way" does not say that a loopback bind blocks remote clients whatever the firewall allows.
findings.evidence: Bound to 127.0.0.1: unreachable either way
findings.fix: Reword to "Bound to 127.0.0.1: remote clients cannot connect even if the firewall allows the port".

findings.summary: The timeout check points to a command that does not test for a firewall drop.
findings.evidence: Timeout | Firewall or security group drops packets, or bad route | ip route get IP
findings.fix: Add a firewall check next to the route check, for example "sudo ufw status; check the security group".

findings.summary: The reachability code block has no one-line note saying what each command is for, unlike the other tables on the page.
findings.evidence:
ping -c 4 host
nc -zv host port
curl -v URL
curl -sI URL
curl -w '%{http_code}' -o /dev/null -s URL
findings.fix: Turn it into a Command | Answers table, or add a short comment to each line.
